items.description_text: Drawing Inclusion through Comics for Youth Work “Drawing Inclusion through Comics for Youth Work” is an international Erasmus+ training course for youth workers, trainers, educators, facilitators and active volunteers working in the fields of non-formal learning and youth work. The training will take place in Munich, Germany, from 28 August to 5 September 2026, including seven activity days and two travel days. It will bring together 34 participants from eight partner organisations in Germany, Spain, Romania, France, Italy, Portugal, the Netherlands and Türkiye. The activity aims to strengthen the quality, innovation and inclusiveness of youth work by introducing digital comics and visual storytelling as practical tools for non-formal education. Participants will learn how to use Web 2.0 platforms such as Pixton, Canva and StoryboardThat to create engaging educational materials and activities for young people. The training is particularly relevant for applicants who work directly with young people with fewer opportunities, including refugees, migrants, NEETs, young people from rural areas, vocational students and those facing social, educational, economic, cultural or geographical barriers. items.description_text: Mindful Youth Work Mosaic is an Erasmus+ Training Course designed for youth workers, mentors, educators, and practitioners from eight European countries who want to explore how mindfulness, body-focused practices, outdoor learning, and experiential education can strengthen personal well-being and improve the quality of youth work. The project addresses current challenges faced by youth workers, including stress, emotional exhaustion, and burnout, by providing practical tools for self-care, resilience, emotional balance, and sustainable approaches to working with young people. Through the unique Outdoor Mosaic process, participants will explore, adapt, and create youth work methods that combine mindfulness, conscious movement, reflection, and outdoor experiential learning. The training will encourage participants to learn by doing, exchange good practices, test activities in an international environment, and reflect on how these approaches can be transferred to their local youth work contexts. The programme combines non-formal education methods, peer learning, outdoor activities, group reflection, body-focused practices, and creative cooperation. Participants will not only gain new personal tools for their own well-being but will also develop innovative approaches that can support young people in their communities. As a result of the project, participants will co-create the Mosaic Guide – a practical resource collecting adapted methods and activities that can be used by youth workers across Europe. The project aims to create long-term impact by strengthening cooperation among partner organisations, encouraging further use of developed tools, and promoting more mindful, resilient, and sustainable youth work practices. Main objectives: Strengthen youth workers’ well-being and resilience by equipping participants with practical mindfulness, body-focused, and self-care tools to prevent burnout and support emotional balance. items.description_text: Since 2024, Link has been implementing the series of projects Youth Work’s Worth, dedicated to enhancing the quality of youth work and strengthening the European youth work ecosystem. During the first edition, the informal BroCoLink Network was established, creating a space for exchange and cooperation among youth organisations. The second edition, held in 2025, laid the foundations for new strategic partnerships and long-term collaboration between participating organisations. The 2026 edition is dedicated to empowering a new generation of youth leaders, equipping them with the knowledge, skills, and competencies needed to address the contemporary challenges facing youth work and to contribute to a stronger, more innovative, and more resilient European youth work community. Since 2020, Link has been an accredited NGO for implementing Erasmus+ and European Solidarity Corps projects. Participants will experiment with creating learning environments that are responsive, engaging and adapted to the real needs of groups instead of relying on fixed methods. items.description_text: This training course is designed for experienced youth workers, educators, trainers, and other helping professionals who work with young people experiencing increased vulnerability and complex life challenges. The course focuses on strengthening participants' capacity to create safer, more inclusive, and supportive environments by integrating three complementary approaches: safeguarding, trauma-informed practice, and solution-focused approaches. We define highly vulnerable young people as those facing at least two significant life challenges, with at least one being chronic, systemic, or particularly difficult to overcome. These challenges may include poverty, abuse, discrimination, family instability, mental health difficulties, neglect, violence, or social exclusion. Supporting these young people requires approaches that recognise the impact of adversity while promoting safety, empowerment, participation, and positive development. Throughout the training, participants will explore: the principles of safeguarding and child protection; risk assessment and creating safer organisational practices; codes of conduct and ethical decision-making; trauma-informed approaches and the impact of adverse childhood experiences (ACEs); psychological first aid and responding to distress; solution-focused approaches that build on strengths, resilience, and young people's existing resources. The programme combines theory with practical tools, reflection, experiential learning, and peer exchange, enabling participants to transfer their learning directly into their everyday practice. The final two days of the programme will take place as part of the Source Conference in Hatvan, where participants will join workshops and learning sessions alongside youth workers, trainers, educators, and other professionals from across Europe. items.description_text: Out with the Burnout vol. 3 is a training course for youth workers, trainers, mentors and staff of youth organisations who work directly with young people — including those facing additional barriers. This activity is specifically targeted at practitioners active in the field of non-formal learning and youth work, who are looking for practical, embodied tools rather than theory alone. Burnout is one of the most under-addressed challenges in youth work: the emotional demands of supporting young people, often with limited resources and time, take a real toll on those doing the supporting. This training gives participants a full week to step back, recognise the early signs of burnout, and build sustainable self-care habits — using non-formal education methods, coaching techniques, movement and body-awareness practices, group reflection and peer support. Across the week, participants will explore where burnout comes from, exchange experiences with peers from partner countries, and practise recovery techniques first-hand rather than just discussing them. items.description_text: Infopack We are living in times of constant connection, yet many of us feel increasingly unsafe in our relationships: misunderstood, unseen, or unable to fully express what is true for us. Whether in our work with others or in our personal lives, we often carry invisible tensions: the fear of being too much or not enough, the habit of self-censoring, the uncertainty of how to respond when emotions arise — our own or someone else’s. Over time, this erodes trust, drains energy, and limits the depth of connection we long for. Emotional safety is not something that simply happens; it is something we learn, practice, and embody. It is the foundation that allows honesty without fear, vulnerability without collapse, and difference without disconnection. When emotional safety is present, people can think more clearly, relate more openly, and act with greater integrity. Without it, even the best tools, intentions, or projects struggle to truly take root. For those working with people — educators, facilitators, youth workers, activists — the ability to create emotional safety is not just a “soft skill,” but a core competence. It shapes the quality of every interaction, every group process, every moment of transformation. And yet, most of us were never taught how to do this in a grounded, embodied way. This is where the journey begins: by turning inward, developing awareness of our own patterns, and learning how to stay present in moments that usually trigger reactivity or withdrawal. From there, we begin to relate differently — with more clarity, compassion, and choice. Emotional Safety Academy invites you into this process: not as a concept to understand, but as a lived experience to cultivate and carry into the spaces and communities you care about. Infopack

This interactive online webinar explores one of the core polarity pairs of the Polarities of Democracy framework, developed by Dr. William Benet. The session will focus on the relationship between diversity and equality, examining why both are essential for democratic societies and how balancing these values can strengthen democratic institutions, participation, and decision-making. The webinar will be led by Stanimir Kiskinov, Fellow of the Institute for the Polarities of Democracy, who will introduce participants to the theoretical foundations of this polarity while encouraging dialogue, critical reflection, and the exchange of experiences. The activity is designed for youth workers, youth leaders, trainers, educators, facilitators, civil society representatives, and other professionals working in the field of non-formal learning and youth work, as well as anyone interested in democracy, civic participation, and social change. Using interactive methods, discussion, and practical examples, participants will: explore the concepts of justice and due process within democratic systems; reflect on current democratic challenges from the perspective of polarity thinking; exchange experiences with participants from different countries and professional backgrounds; discover how the Polarities of Democracy framework can be applied in youth work, non-formal education, and community engagement. In a world where it’s easy to lose connection, many of us are looking for ways to feel grounded, seen, and real. We all carry stories, shaped not only by what we say, but also by how we move, speak, and show up for one another. YOUnisphere invites youth workers into this living sphere: a space where embodiment and storytelling become tools to activate, engage, and empower. We start from personal experience and translate it into practical tools that can be used to support others and shape meaningful learning spaces. Disclaimer: This program is offered as a learning and training experience. It focuses on practical tools, reflection, and shared exploration. It is not therapy, and it is not intended to replace professional mental health care or clinical support. THE METHODOLOGIES We experience reality, and life, through our body. We make sense of it through the stories we tell ourselves and each other. Embodiment invites us to discover how the body holds and expresses memory, emotion, and presence. Through movement, creative dance, vocal activities, meditation and reflective practices, we learn how fully showing up in our bodies can strengthen confidence, deepen connection, and make communication more authentic. Applied storytelling explores how stories shape the way we see ourselves and others. We don’t just tell stories, we inhabit them, letting them guide us, stretch us, and connect us. We practice crafting and sharing stories in ways that engage, inspire, and foster empathy through our imagination, traditional and personal stories. items.description_text: Wise Elders Village is an experiential Erasmus+ training course for youth workers who long to rediscover one of humanity’s oldest ways of accompanying growth: the village. There was a time when every young person crossed life’s thresholds held by community, ceremony, and the wisdom of Elders. Today, many of these rites of passage have disappeared, leaving young people to navigate profound transitions alone. Wise Elders Village is an invitation to remember how communities can once again become places where belonging is cultivated, unique gifts are witnessed, and young people are supported in becoming fully human. During seven days immersed in the wilderness of Southern Italy, participants will not simply learn new methodologies. They will experience from within a contemporary village inspired by rites of passage, discovering what it means to be held by community before learning how to hold others in return. The training weaves together nature connection, the Way of Council, ceremony, symbolic work, embodiment, storytelling, silence, community practices, and a 24-hour solo threshold in nature, rooted in the contemporary tradition of rites of passage. Rather than transmitting techniques, the course invites participants to embody these practices so they may accompany young people with greater presence, discernment, and wisdom. At the heart of the journey lies the question: How can we become the villages our young people have been longing for? By remembering the role of the Elder—not as someone who possesses answers, but as one who knows how to witness, listen deeply, hold community, and bless the unique path of each young person. The experience culminates in a 24-hour solo threshold in nature, offering participants the opportunity to cross their own symbolic passage before returning to the village carrying the gifts discovered along the way. Series – The Game Changer: From Board Games to Learning in Youth Work.” Turn a Game into Learning Why reinvent the wheel when the world of board games already offers an incredible toolbox for learning, reflection, and growth? items.description_text: An experiential online lab for trainers and youth workers that combines the spirit of Ask Better, Teach Better with the creative tools of Play to Learn. Participants start from their own practice: each small group brings one concrete issue from their work with young people (for example participation, conflict, online behaviour, inclusion, or the impact of AI). Every game is treated as a new question: an invitation for young people to explore “What is really happening here?” and “What could we do differently?” through play. The focus is on low‑tech, easy‑to‑run games that can be prototyped and facilitated with very simple materials: scarves, balls and objects that participants can either create themselves or find easily in nature or their immediate environment (stones, sticks, leaves, paper, recycled items). items.title: Outdoor Paths: Designing Experiential Activities for Young People
items.summary: An online workshop for youth workers to design safe, inclusive outdoor learning journeys. Using visual “island–storm–harbour” maps, participants turn real group needs into structured outdoor games, reflection walks and community‑based challenges.

items.description_text: This online workshop is designed for youth workers who already use games and activities with young people and want to upgrade them into well‑designed outdoor and experiential learning processes. Instead of offering a random collection of icebreakers, the training focuses on how to: turn real issues from youth work (group tension, low participation, stress, intercultural challenges) into outdoor and experiential activities plan activities that are safe, inclusive and purposeful in very different local contexts – from small neighbourhood parks to busy city centres. Participants work with a simple “learning journey” metaphor (island – wind – storms – harbour – legacy) to map what supports and what blocks them when they plan outdoor learning with young people. Building on this, they learn a step‑by‑step planning model: Define a clear learning focus (e.g. trust, communication, dealing with uncertainty, reconnecting with nature). Choose and analyse a real space they have access to (street, park, school yard, seaside, village square). Design an activity that uses this space as a co‑facilitator: routes, objects, landmarks and people become part of the game or challenge. items.description_text: A practical online workshop designed for youth workers, trainers and educators who want to explore educational robotics as a tool for learning. The focus is on how robots and simple programmable devices can support skills such as collaboration, planning, resilience and systems thinking. Participants explore what “robotics” can look like in youth work: from programmable toys and simple kits to low‑tech simulations of robots when no hardware is available. Through concrete examples, the session introduces the idea of mission‑based activities: small challenges where a “robot” has to achieve a goal (follow a line, move an object, navigate a map, simulate a social scenario). Participants see how each mission can be framed around real‑life issues, such as accessibility, environmental protection, or community problem‑solving, turning robotics into a vehicle for values and discussion. In groups, participants design one robotics session tailored to their own context and resources. They choose a mission, define roles within the team (e.g. programmer, builder, tester, documenter), and outline the steps from briefing to testing to debriefing. They also plan how they will handle mistakes and failures as learning moments, and how they will invite all young people to contribute, regardless of technical confidence. The workshop concludes with presentations of the session plans, peer feedback and a short reflection on how robotics can connect to broader youth work goals, such as inclusion, participation and digital literacy. So how can we intentionally create youth spaces that truly Connect, Inform and Empower? Throughout the training, participants will exchange good practices, test and refine facilitation methods, and contribute to the development of a practical youth work resource that can be transferred into their everyday youth work practice. Young women living in rural and peripheral areas experience unique realities that present both opportunities and challenges. Rural communities often offer strong social connections, a sense of belonging and growing spaces for community engagement, local leadership and social innovation. At the same time, young women may face barriers such as geographical isolation, limited mobility, reduced access to information, fewer educational and professional opportunities, persistent gender stereotypes and less direct access to youth services and international experiences. These factors can particularly affect young women with fewer opportunities, influencing their participation in community life and their awareness of, and access to, local, national and European opportunities. Youth work has an important role to play in recognising the strengths of rural communities while addressing the barriers that prevent young women from fully participating, accessing information and benefiting from the opportunities available to them. Youth workers and youth organisations play an important role in addressing these inequalities. They can create inclusive spaces, provide information, accompany young women in accessing opportunities and develop practices that respond to the realities of their communities. The PBA will bring together youth workers from E+ and ESC Programme and Southern Mediterranean countries to exchange experiences and reflect on how their organisations engage young women, remove barriers and make opportunities more visible, accessible and inclusive. For example, as indicated by the YPS monitoring (Dr. Dan Moxon, YPS Steering group, 2024), between 2021 and 2023, only 9.8% of participants in Erasmus+ Youth projects with participation themes were young people with fewer opportunities (YPFO) (considerably lower than the 30% of estimated participants in Erasmus+ KA1 activities (Youth Exchanges, Youth Workers Mobility and Youth Participation activities) who are YPFO). Youth workers, educators, and trainers are key actors in supporting these young people, but they often lack practical tools and knowledge to address the specific challenges these youth face when engaging in democratic life. This study visit is part of a long-term project organised by SALTO Inclusion & Diversity and SALTO Participation & Information, which aims to strengthen competences to design and facilitate inclusive, accessible, and meaningful democratic participation processes with diverse groups of young people. items.description_text: Across Europe, democratic values are increasingly under pressure, and public discourse is becoming more polarised. Amid these developments, youth work stands at a crossroads: socially and politically relevant enough to matter yet increasingly expected to remain “apolitical” and focus on individual life skills. Youth work practitioners often find themselves navigating difficult dilemmas, such as how youth work can operate effectively in politically volatile and polarised environments, what its role is in safeguarding democracy, and whether depoliticisation is a viable response or itself a political choice. And if not, how can youth workers navigate the risks and responsibilities of taking a stand for democracy? The seminar targets youth work practitioners who want to strengthen democratic values and attitudes amongst their target group and within their communities, and exchange ideas and experiences with like-minded colleagues. In particular, the seminar aims to offer a space for youth work practitioners to: -explore the current state of democracy and better understand its implications for youth work and young people's lives; -reflect on the ethical and political dimensions of youth work and its role in promoting and sustaining democratic values; -examine existing projects, initiatives, and practices that have responded to democratic backsliding and critically reflect on what worked well and what was less effective; -enable and support participants in finding the right approach in their youth work to strengthen and support democratic values in their local context; -encourage participants to develop concrete follow-up activities for their local youth work and communities. items.title: PLAY IS HUMAN RIGHT – The neuroscience of joy and the NVC practice of connection
items.summary: Inspired by Jaak Panksepp’s affective neuroscience and Nonviolent Communication (NVC), this webinar explores how the PLAY system supports connection, resilience, creativity, and emotional wellbeing.
items.participants_countries: Erasmus+ Youth Programme countries , Other countries in the world , Partner Countries Neighbouring the EU
items.fee_text: no
items.description_text: In Jaak Panksepp’s affective neuroscience, PLAY is one of the brain’s primary emotional systems—a neural circuit that supports connection, flexibility, learning, resilience, and social trust. And yet, in many adult lives, especially in work, parenting, leadership, and intimate relationships, play often disappears first. During this webinar, we will explore the PLAY circuit through the lens of Nonviolent Communication (NVC). Together, we will discover why play requires a sense of safety, how joy differs from entertainment or performance, and how a playful presence can soften tension, open space for dialogue, and support our needs for connection, freedom, creativity, ease, and belonging. We will also ask: What happens to our relationships when play is absent? Why do we sometimes lose access to lightness, curiosity, and spontaneity? How can sharing NVC help us bring play back without forcing it, bypassing pain, or pretending everything is okay? Where playfulness can support sharing and learning NVC? This webinar is for people who want to understand play not as a luxury, but as a deep human need and a powerful doorway to empathy, regulation, and more alive relationships. It is a result of the Erasmus + training course “Flying Giraffes” that took place in Poland in June 2026. You can register here: https://www.fundacjamudita.org/en/play-is-human-right-the-neuroscience-of-joy-and-the-nvc-practice-of-connection-with-paulina-orbitowska-fernandez/

items.description_text: How do we break through the paralysis of crisis fatigue and reclaim our power to act in a world that feels increasingly out of our control? We are living through times of ecological, social, and political crisis. Geopolitical tensions, deep societal divisions, and environmental changes have created a heavy, exhausting sense of uncertainty. For many young people, this does not just cause worry—it leads to a deep feeling that nothing they do matters, causing them to fall into disengagement, frustration, and social withdrawal. But waiting for the uncertainty to pass is not an option. This training course is a direct call to move past passive concern and step into active, collective initiative. items.description_text: How can innovation and research help shape a more effective, inclusive and impactful Erasmus+ and the European Solidarity Corps? Rather than treating learning as a rigid line—plan, teach, test, finish—it treats learning as an ongoing cycle of experimentation, feedback, reflection, and self-direction. items.description_text: Das Training richtet sich an Fachkräfte der Jugendarbeit sowie an Entscheidungsträgerinnen und Entscheidungsträger, die sich mit der Gestaltung, Entwicklung und politischen Rahmung von Räumen für junge Menschen befassen. Ziel des Trainings ist es, neue Perspektiven auf jugendgerechte Orte zu eröffnen und innovative Modelle kennenzulernen, die Begegnung, Austausch und selbstbestimmte Nutzung ermöglichen. Ausgangspunkt bildet der in Luxemburg formulierte Bedarf junger Menschen nach frei zugänglichen, sicheren und attraktiven Orten, an denen sie sich treffen, Zeit miteinander verbringen, Erlebnisse teilen und Erfahrungen sammeln können. Das Training greift diesen Bedarf auf und lädt dazu ein, das Angebot an Räumen für Jugendliche neu zu denken und weiterzuentwickeln. Im Rahmen des Trainings werden europäische Praxisbeispiele aus Belgien, Südtirol, der Schweiz und Deutschland vorgestellt. Sie zeigen, wie Räume für junge Menschen in unterschiedlichen Kontexten gestaltet und betrieben werden können. Ergänzend werden die luxemburgischen Rahmenbedingungen beleuchtet. Die Teilnehmenden haben die Möglichkeit, sich mit Vertreterinnen und Vertretern der vorgestellten Organisationen auszutauschen und Einblicke in deren Arbeitsweisen, Herausforderungen und Erfolgsfaktoren zu gewinnen. Ein weiterer Programmpunkt ist die Besichtigung eines vom nationalen Jugenddienst geführten Maker Space. Die Teilnehmenden lernen vor Ort ein konkretes Praxisbeispiel kennen und können sich mit den verantwortlichen Fachkräften austauschen. Das Training bietet Raum für Reflexion, Diskussion und Vernetzung. Es unterstützt die Teilnehmenden dabei, neue Ansätze kennenzulernen und Anregungen für die eigene Praxis mitzunehmen. Ziel ist es, Impulse für die Weiterentwicklung jugendgerechter Räume in Europa zu setzen und Angebote nachhaltig an den Bedürfnissen junger Menschen auszurichten.

For details please check the "Costs" section which is located on the right side of this page. Description Sport is much more than just physical activity. It is also a powerful tool for promoting social inclusion, empowering young people from disadvantaged backgrounds and encouraging their active participation in society. During this activity, participants will visit organisations that use sport as a tool for social inclusion, youth empowerment and community development. The programme will also include dedicated partnership-building sessions designed to foster sustainable international cooperation and support the development of future Erasmus+ projects. Objectives: To observe and learn from good practices implemented by organisations using sport as a tool for social inclusion; To improve the knowledge and know-how of sport staff; To exchange experiences, approaches and methods through peer learning; To establish sustainable international partnerships; To explore opportunities for developing future cooperation projects within the Erasmus+ Mobility of Staff in the field of Sport. Target Group: Youth workers, athletes, coaches, trainers, volunteers, staff and representatives of organisations working in the fields of sport, primarily in grassroot sport, social inclusion and related areas, particularly organisations using sport for social purposes rather than for professional or competitive purposes; Participants who are motivated to establish international partnerships and develop future Erasmus+ cooperation projects; Participants who are able to communicate and work effectively in English.

items.description_text: Are you a youth leader or youth worker committed to becoming an agent of change in your local community and beyond? Are you interested in learning more about what quality youth participation means and how you can embed it in your organisational life or the new projects that you plan? Do you want to explore the opportunities of the Erasmus+ Programme? Then “Dive into Youth Participation” is the Training Course for you! Youth participation in democratic life and young people's active civic engagement are high priorities of the EU Youth Strategy and are incorporated into the majority of contemporary youth policy frameworks in different European countries. The Erasmus+ Programme is one of the mechanisms to put the EU Youth Strategy into practice and provide many opportunities for young people to develop international projects, which empower them to take an active role in society and help them develop civic and social competencies. In this context, the fourth edition of the Training Course “Dive into Youth Participation” brings together 25 youth leaders and youth workers from different European countries with an aim to improve their understanding and practices toward quality youth participation. This is also an opportunity to learn more about the possibilities within the Erasmus+ Key Action 154 “Youth Participation Activities” and how to ensure youth participation is properly implemented in all stages of a project or participation initiative. Profile of participants The call is open for youth leaders and youth workers who fit the following criteria: -representatives of youth/youth work organisations or informal groups of young people; -have experience with youth participation or civic engagement; -are interested in developing projects within the Erasmus+ Key Action 154 “Youth Participation Activities” (no prior experience is required); -are interested in developing/improving youth participation practices/projects at any level (local, national, European or international)

items.description_text: NGO Awero team, Nexes Interculturals, Cities of Learning Network partners, and the International Youth Work Trainers Guild are offering a 6th modular training for trainers, aligned to the European Training Strategy (ETS) competence model. The training course will contribute to the development of the ETS trainers’ competences in the area of “Being Civically Engaged”. Understanding and asserting the trainer's work as an act of civic engagement Connecting relevant [youth] policies and educational programmes to own values, beliefs and different political perspectives Reflecting on personal civic engagement, values and beliefs, and integrating them in the training practice in a responsible and constructive way Supporting learners in developing critical thinking and using the diversity of opinions and beliefs as a source of learning Applying democracy and human rights principles in the design and delivery of training activities. Programme of the training course The programme opens with introductions, setting the learning stage, and exploring participants' personal values and beliefs, then links these to trainer identity and active citizenship. Midweek, the group will travel to Barcelona to explore civic engagement and local training practices, including a Migrantour optional session in one of Barcelona’s neighbourhoods. The later days shift to developing pilot civically engaged training practice ideas, examining diversity, democracy and human rights as sources of learning, and covering resources for trainers' professional development and recognition. Please check the draft programme attached to this call for participants. items.description_text: This course is a self-paced, interactive, practical course for Youth Workers to learn how to support groups of youth with fewer/less opportunities in creating and realizing their own volunteering projects and use it as an experiential learning process for the volunteers. It is a Beta version, please provide your feedback on the feedback forms incorparated into the course, to help us make it as good and useful as possible! You are going to learn about: - how to approach youth with fewer/less opportunities, - how to mobilize and recruit them to create their own volunteer projects, - how to work with them, - how to inspire, connect, empower, coach and mentor them in this process. About this course: In this course, you have a chance to learn about supporting youth with fewer/less opportunities who come from minority or socially disadvantaged background in the context of youth work. More specifically you can learn about how to support a group of youth with fewer/less opportunities in a non-formal learning program that is based on volunteering. The above-mentioned topics are explored by sharing and expanding a field-tested practice of working with Hungarian youth living in foster care and in segregated minority communities run since 2011. This method is called: From Us to You (FUY/FUYI - but we like to pronounce it FUJI). Aims and objectives of the course: The course aims to introduce the elements of the From Us to You program that make a volunteering based non-formal education program effective. By doing so we would like to share what we have found useful in our work in supporting youth with fewer/less opportunities. Besides our learnings, we also share the resources and approaches we have learned from within or outside of the field of youth work. More concretely, you will have a short glimpse into: - Experiential education - Solution focused approach - Trauma informed approach. items.description_text: How can international youth mobility become truly safe, inclusive, and empowering for Highly Vulnerable Young People? A course for youth workers, facilitators, and organisations to learn how to create safer, more inclusive, and trauma-informed international mobility experiences for Highly Vulnerable Young People (HVYP). This is a self-paced and practice-oriented online course for professionals working in youth mobility and non-formal education. The course supports participants in developing the competencies needed to responsibly include and support young people facing multiple and intersecting barriers in international programmes. You are going to learn about: safer and more inclusive mobility environments, safeguarding and risk management in practice, trauma-informed and solution-focused approaches, recognising and preventing harm and exclusion, supporting HVYP before, during, and after mobility experiences, professional boundaries, crisis response, and self-care in youth work. About this course International youth mobility projects can create powerful opportunities for learning, participation, connection, and personal growth. At the same time, for highly vulnerable young people, unfamiliar international environments may also involve increased vulnerability and risk. This course was developed within the LADDER project to support youth workers and organisations in creating mobility experiences that are not only accessible, but genuinely safe, supportive, and empowering. Through practical examples, case studies, reflection exercises, and field-tested approaches, participants will strengthen their capacity to: create safer and more inclusive mobility projects, anticipate and prevent risks, respond responsibly to challenging situations, and support young people facing multiple barriers. items.description_text: The project arises from a shared observation among young people, community development professionals, and partner organizations: a growing need to reconnect with the living world, rebuild social bonds, and collectively reflect on current ecological challenges in the face of the climate emergency. It addresses two main needs: Strengthening the skills of facilitators and community leaders so they can design and implement educational projects with strong social and ecological impact. Actively engaging young people in meaningful, concrete, and transformative projects. The project uses the living garden as an educational, sensory, and cooperative tool, helping to recreate connections between humans and ecosystems. These spaces become platforms for social transformation, civic education, and territorial resilience. It is based on active pedagogy that promotes autonomy, local engagement, and the transversal skills required for the ecological transition. The event will take place outdoors and is aimed at educators, activity leaders, and facilitators. In Brittany, 27 participants are expected.
